summary: Monitorability has concept-level, monitor-relative definitions: Anwar et al. 2026 define it as the Bayes-optimal accuracy uplift, bounded by I(Y;Z|X), with a V-information variant. Baker et al. 2025 define faithfulness as sufficiency and legibility as recoverability by a monitor. Mohammadkhani et al. 2026 prove that covert computation must leak into the CoT but may be unreadable by polynomial-time monitors. Outside ML, runtime-verification monitorability and DES diagnosability/opacity are formal observer-relative notions. Legibility/checkability is formal as completeness plus soundness against a verifier (Kirchner, Anil, self-proving models, debate) and as observer goal inference (Dragan; Kulkarni's k/j-goal obfuscation and legibility). Steganography has classical security definitions (Cachin, Hopper, de Witt) that require a cover distribution. Anwar, Piskorz et al. 2026 instead define it as a positive Receiver-minus-Sentinel gap in usable information. Unifying candidate: usable information relative to observer classes (V-information). None of these is causal except one monitorability bound.

candidates.title: A Decision-Theoretic Formalisation of Steganography With Applications to LLM Monitoring
candidates.authors: Usman Anwar, Julianna Piskorz, David D. Baek, David Africa, Jim Weatherall, Max Tegmark, Christian Schroeder de Witt, Mihaela van der Schaar, David Krueger
candidates.formalism: decision theory; generalised V-information (usable information relative to a decoder class)
candidates.formal_object: Steganographic gap: the usable information a signal Z gives a Receiver decoder class minus what it gives a trusted Sentinel class, on an auditing task (Y,u). Z counts as steganographic iff the gap is positive.
candidates.key_formula: \Delta_{\mathrm{steg}}(Z)=I_{\mathrm{rec}}(Z\to Y)-I_{\mathrm{sen}}(Z\to Y),\quad I^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Z\to Y\mid X)=U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X,Z)-U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X),\quad U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X)=\sup_{d\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbb{E}[u(Y,d[X])]
candidates.assumptions: Decoder classes V_rec and V_sen; a Sentinel matched in capability but without the key; an auditing task with ground truth Y and utility u; observable downstream decisions. No covertext distribution needed.
candidates.relevance: The only definition of steganographic reasoning that needs no reference distribution. Steganography is relative to a monitor class and a task. Recovers Cachin's epsilon-security as a special case (App. D). Template for monitor-relative definitions.

candidates.title: A Theory of Usable Information Under Computational Constraints
candidates.authors: Yilun Xu, Shengjia Zhao, Jiaming Song, Russell Stewart, Stefano Ermon
candidates.formalism: variational information theory (predictive V-information)
candidates.formal_object: Predictive V-information: the reduction in the best log loss that a constrained predictor family V gets from seeing Z. Unlike Shannon information, it can be created by computation and destroyed by encryption.
candidates.key_formula: I_{\mathcal{V}}(Z\to Y\mid X)=H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X)-H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X,Z),\quad H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X)=\inf_{d\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbb{E}[-\log d[X](Y)] \text{ (as restated in arXiv 2602.23163, Eqs. 1-3)}
candidates.assumptions: A predictive family V that satisfies optional ignorance; a joint distribution over (X, Y, Z); log loss, or a utility in the generalised version.
candidates.relevance: The common primitive behind monitor-relative monitorability (Anwar et al. 2026, App. E), the steganographic gap and REV (in the map). Lets 'illegible' and 'encoded' be defined as information that exists but is not usable by a monitor class.

candidates.title: Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory
candidates.authors: Usman Anwar, Tim Bakker, Dana Kianfar, Cristina Pinneri, Christos Louizos
candidates.formalism: information theory; Bayes-optimal monitors; V-information (App. E)
candidates.formal_object: CoT monitorability of an attribute Y: the accuracy uplift of the Bayes-optimal CoT monitor over the prompt-only monitor. Bounded by conditional MI. A practical monitor's error splits into information gap and elicitation error.
candidates.assumptions: A ground-truth output monitor g that defines the attribute; the policy distribution pi(O|X,Z); a monitor hypothesis class V for the practical version.
candidates.relevance: The closest existing concept-level formal definition of CoT monitorability, relative to an attribute and (in App. E) to a monitor class. Purely observational: MI > 0 is satisfied by post-hoc CoTs too (Remark 3.11).

candidates.title: Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
candidates.authors: Bowen Baker, Joost Huizinga, Leo Gao, Zehao Dou, Melody Y. Guan, Aleksander Madry, Wojciech Zaremba, Jakub Pachocki, David Farhi
candidates.formalism: statistics (sufficient statistic); monitor-relative recoverability
candidates.formal_object: A latent z (e.g. a CoT) is faithful w.r.t. output property v iff z is a sufficient statistic for v. It is legible to monitor M iff M can predict v from z. Monitor success implies both.
candidates.assumptions: A target property v of outputs; a joint distribution over latent and output; a specific monitor M for legibility. Stated verbally in §5.1, with no formula.
candidates.relevance: Splits monitorability into a monitor-free part (sufficiency, faithfulness) and a monitor-relative part (legibility). This is the same split as Shannon information vs V-information, and the natural starting point for a causal refinement.

candidates.title: Hidden Reasoning Must Leak, but Need Not Be Readable: Fundamental Opportunities and Limits for Chain-of-Thought Monitoring
candidates.authors: Mohammadali Mohammadkhani, Madhava Krishna, Yash Sarrof, Michael Hahn
candidates.formalism: circuit complexity of fixed-precision transformers; information theory; cryptography (NC0 pseudo-random generators)
candidates.formal_object: Information-theoretic footprint I[X_covert; CoT] of covert computation. Thm 3.1: beyond model capacity the footprint must be near-linear. Thm 3.5: a 1-layer transformer can encrypt its CoT so that no polynomial-time monitor beats chance.
candidates.key_formula: I[X_{\mathrm{covert}},\mathrm{CoT}]=\tilde{\Omega}(N)\ \text{whenever }|\mathrm{CoT}|\text{ is polynomially bounded in }N:=|X_{\mathrm{covert}}|\ \text{(Eq. 3, transcribed from PDF)}
candidates.assumptions: Fixed-precision transformer; specific state-tracking and arithmetic tasks with a uniform covert input; greedy decoding; Thm 3.5 needs an unproven NC0 PRG assumption.
candidates.relevance: Formally separates leakage (Shannon) from readability (computationally bounded monitors). A definition of monitorability or encoded reasoning must therefore be relative to a monitor class, not stated in raw mutual information.

candidates.title: An Information-Theoretic Model for Steganography
candidates.authors: Christian Cachin
candidates.venue: Information Hiding Workshop 1998; revised version in Information and Computation (2004)
candidates.formalism: information theory; hypothesis testing
candidates.formal_object: Security of a stegosystem against a passive warden: the relative entropy between covertext and stegotext distributions, which bounds any detector. epsilon-secure if it is at most epsilon, perfectly secure if it is zero.
candidates.key_formula: D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{1}\|P_{0})\leq\varepsilon\ \text{(as restated in arXiv 2602.23163, App. D; the abstract states the relative entropy between the distributions of } C \text{ and } S)
candidates.assumptions: A known covertext distribution; a passive adversary; the detection task framed as hypothesis testing.
candidates.relevance: The classical security definition. Encoded-reasoning definitions must either supply a covertext distribution (an 'honest CoT' distribution, unavailable for LLMs) or replace it, as the decision-theoretic gap does.

candidates.title: Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs
candidates.authors: Jan Hendrik Kirchner, Yining Chen, Harri Edwards, Jan Leike, Nat McAleese, Yuri Burda
candidates.formalism: interactive-proof-style completeness and soundness relative to a verifier and a prover model family
candidates.formal_object: Checkability (verifiability) of prover pi to verifier v on P_XY. Completeness: correct outputs are accepted. Soundness: no prover in family H gets an incorrect output accepted. Legibility is checkability in practice.
candidates.assumptions: A ground-truth correctness label; a verifier class (small models or time-limited humans); an adversarial prover family H.
candidates.relevance: The standard formal definition of legibility/checkability for CoT. It concerns correctness of the answer, not whether the CoT reflects the computation. Contrasting it with faithfulness is needed.

candidates.title: Opacity in Discrete Event Systems: A Perspective and Overview
candidates.authors: Xiang Yin
candidates.formalism: partially observed automata; state estimation; hyperproperties (HyperLTL)
candidates.formal_object: Opacity: an observer can never know for sure that the system is, was, or will be in a secret state (current-state, initial-state, K-step variants). Diagnosability is the dual: a fault is always inferred within finite delay.
candidates.assumptions: A known system model (automaton or Petri net); an observation map such as a natural projection; a secret set of states or language; worst-case (possibilistic) or stochastic inference.
candidates.relevance: A mature formal framework that covers several concepts at once. Diagnosability is formal monitorability ('always eventually know'), opacity is formal obfuscation ('always not know'), and both are unified as hyperproperties. Points to Lin 2011 and Sampath et al. 1995.

candidates.title: Provably Secure Steganography
candidates.authors: Nicholas J. Hopper, John Langford, Luis von Ahn
candidates.venue: CRYPTO 2002 (extended abstract); full version IACR ePrint 2002/137
candidates.formalism: complexity theory; computational indistinguishability
candidates.formal_object: Steganographic security against a computationally bounded warden: stegotexts are computationally indistinguishable from covertexts drawn from a channel. Secure stegosystems exist if one-way functions exist.
candidates.assumptions: Sampling access to the covertext channel; a shared secret key; polynomial-time adversaries.
candidates.relevance: The computational counterpart of Cachin. With Mohammadkhani et al. it shows that undetectability by bounded monitors is the relevant notion for encoded CoT. It still needs a cover distribution and a shared key.

candidates.title: Perfectly Secure Steganography Using Minimum Entropy Coupling
candidates.authors: Christian Schroeder de Witt, Samuel Sokota, J. Zico Kolter, Jakob Foerster, Martin Strohmeier
candidates.formalism: information theory (couplings, minimum entropy coupling)
candidates.formal_object: Characterization: a steganography procedure is perfectly secure under Cachin's model iff it is induced by a coupling. Among those, it maximizes throughput iff induced by a minimum entropy coupling.
candidates.assumptions: Cachin's model with a known covertext distribution, here given by a generative model such as GPT-2; a shared key.
candidates.relevance: Shows that perfectly undetectable encoding in LLM text is achievable. Distribution-based detection of encoded reasoning therefore cannot work in principle, which motivates behavioural, monitor-relative definitions.

candidates.title: Learning to Give Checkable Answers with Prover-Verifier Games
candidates.authors: Cem Anil, Guodong Zhang, Yuhuai Wu, Roger Grosse
candidates.formalism: game theory (simultaneous and sequential prover-verifier games, Stackelberg equilibria)
candidates.formal_object: Prover-Verifier Games. A trusted verifier and an untrusted, stronger prover with competing objectives. Identifies the game variants whose equilibria provably yield a sound and complete justification protocol.
candidates.assumptions: A decision problem with ground truth; learner classes for prover and verifier; equilibrium play.
candidates.relevance: The game-theoretic source of Kirchner's checkability definition. It defines checkable answers as an equilibrium property, which fits a definition of legibility relative to a verifier class.

candidates.title: Models That Prove Their Own Correctness
candidates.authors: Noga Amit, Shafi Goldwasser, Orr Paradise, Guy Rothblum
candidates.formalism: interactive proofs; learning theory
candidates.formal_object: Self-Proving model: w.h.p. over inputs from a distribution, it outputs a correct answer and convinces verifier V via an interactive proof. V's soundness guarantees that no model can convince it of an incorrect output on any input.
candidates.assumptions: A verification algorithm V with an interactive proof for the task (e.g. GCD); an input distribution; accepting transcripts or verifier feedback for training.
candidates.relevance: The most rigorous formalization of checkability for learned models: soundness holds for every input and every prover, not just on average. Gives a crypto-grade target for a 'checkable CoT' definition.

candidates.title: AI safety via debate
candidates.authors: Geoffrey Irving, Paul Christiano, Dario Amodei
candidates.formalism: complexity theory (interactive proofs); zero-sum games
candidates.formal_object: Debate: a zero-sum game between two agents judged by a human. With optimal play, debate with polynomial-time judges answers any PSPACE question (direct judging answers only NP).
candidates.assumptions: Optimal play; an honest debater able to simulate the computation; a polynomial-time judge.
candidates.relevance: Frames oversight as which problem classes a weak judge can verify. This is a complexity-theoretic notion of checkability that can be adapted to judge monitorability.

candidates.title: Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate
candidates.authors: Jonah Brown-Cohen, Geoffrey Irving, Georgios Piliouras, Lijie Chen, Jiawei Li, Zhiyang Xun
candidates.formalism: complexity theory; recursive debate protocols
candidates.formal_object: The obfuscated arguments problem: a dishonest debater forces an honest one into an intractable check. A prover-estimator protocol lets the honest debater win with efficiency comparable to the opponent, under stability assumptions.
candidates.assumptions: Recursive problem decomposition; stability assumptions on the subclaim probabilities; computationally bounded debaters.
candidates.relevance: The only formal treatment of argument obfuscation, meaning obfuscation by intractability rather than hiding. Relevant to defining obfuscated CoT relative to a verifier's computational budget.

candidates.title: Games for AI Control: Models of Safety Evaluations of AI Deployment Protocols
candidates.authors: Charlie Griffin, Louis Thomson, Buck Shlegeris, Alessandro Abate
candidates.formalism: game theory (multi-objective partially observable stochastic games)
candidates.formal_object: AI-Control Games between a protocol designer and a red team, which controls a scheming untrusted model. Safety and usefulness of protocols such as Trusted Monitoring are defined as game values, with reductions to zero-sum POSGs.
candidates.assumptions: A scheming untrusted model that knows the protocol; a trusted weaker monitor; a limited human audit budget; specified payoffs.
candidates.relevance: Formalizes oversight as a game against an adversarial policy. It suggests defining monitorability as safety achievable by a monitor class against a worst-case policy class, not on average.

candidates.title: Monitorability of omega-regular languages
candidates.authors: Andreas Bauer
candidates.formalism: formal languages; temporal logic (LTL); runtime verification
candidates.formal_object: Runtime-verification monitorability: a property L is monitorable iff every finite prefix u has a finite extension v after which every infinite continuation is in L, or every one is outside L. Gives the complexity of deciding it.
candidates.key_formula: \forall u\,\exists v:\ (\forall w.\ uvw\in L)\ \lor\ (\forall w.\ uvw\notin L)\ \text{(rendered from the abstract)}
candidates.assumptions: A specification given as an omega-regular language or LTL formula; observation of finite prefixes of an execution.
candidates.relevance: 'Monitorability' already has a precise meaning in formal methods: verdict-determinability from finite observation. The CoT notion differs (inference of a hidden property), so the terminology clash should be addressed.

candidates.title: Legibility and Predictability of Robot Motion
candidates.authors: Anca D. Dragan, Kenton C.T. Lee, Siddhartha S. Srinivasa
candidates.formalism: Bayesian goal inference (inverse planning with a cost-based observer model)
candidates.formal_object: Legibility: the observer infers the correct goal quickly and confidently from a trajectory prefix (action-to-goal inference). Predictability: the trajectory matches the observer's goal-to-action expectation. The two can conflict.
candidates.assumptions: A known goal set; an observer model of rational action with cost function C; a time-weighting f(t).
candidates.relevance: A formal, observer-relative definition of legibility as speed of correct intent inference from a partial trace. It maps directly onto monitoring a CoT prefix for the model's goal. Its legibility/predictability split parallels legibility vs simulatability.

candidates.title: A Unified Framework for Planning in Adversarial and Cooperative Environments
candidates.authors: Anagha Kulkarni, Siddharth Srivastava, Subbarao Kambhampati
candidates.formalism: classical planning with a partially informed observer (observation model, belief over goals)
candidates.formal_object: Goal obfuscation: the plan's observations stay consistent with at least k goals. Goal legibility: they are consistent with at most j goals. Plan obfuscation and plan legibility control what the observer can infer about next actions.
candidates.assumptions: A known observer sensor model mapping action-state pairs to observations; a set of candidate (decoy or confounding) goals; an offline observer.
candidates.relevance: One framework that formally defines obfuscation and legibility as two ends of the same observer-relative quantity. A model for treating CoT obfuscation and legibility jointly.

candidates.title: Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
candidates.authors: Qiang Fu, Xinyue Li, Andre Wibisono, Arman Cohan
candidates.in_map: anon2026improving (likely the same work under a new title; OpenReview version in the map)
candidates.formalism: structural causal models; potential outcomes; partial identification bounds
candidates.formal_object: Causal recall: the probability that the monitor flags a case whose target outcome was caused by the intervention (Y(1)=1, Y(0)=0). The common TPR_mc metric is an upper bound, and a lower bound is derived.
candidates.assumptions: One SCM for both arms, with consistency (Assumption 1); a binary intervention; a binary outcome and monitor decision; p1 > p0.
candidates.relevance: The only causal (SCM/potential-outcome) definition of a monitorability quantity found. It already uses 'necessary cause' structure (Y(0)=0, Y(1)=1) and is directly extensible with Halpern-Pearl actual causation.

candidates.title: Don't Judge an Agent by Its Messages: Private-State Leakage under Passive Monitoring of Agent Communication
candidates.authors: Daksh Pandey, Sayon Duttagupta, Xinhai Zou, Amit Singh Bhati
candidates.formalism: information theory; partial identification of mutual-information leakage from observable laws
candidates.formal_object: What a passive auditor can certify about the leakage of private state through messages. Compatible MI leakage forms a sharp interval. It is determined iff the residual private state or the message is a deterministic function of the task state.
candidates.assumptions: The auditor knows the authorised sender and the exact observable message and outcome law, with no trusted pairing of messages and private states.
candidates.relevance: A formal non-identifiability result: matching an honest sender's observable behaviour cannot rule out covert leakage. It limits any observational, monitor-based definition of steganography.

candidates.title: Quantifying the Necessity of Chain of Thought through Opaque Serial Depth
candidates.authors: Jonah Brown-Cohen, David Lindner, Rohin Shah
candidates.formalism: circuit complexity (circuit depth between designated interpretable nodes)
candidates.formal_object: Opaque serial depth: the length of the longest computation possible without passing through interpretable nodes such as CoT tokens, computed as circuit depth between interpretable nodes. Bounds how much reasoning can stay unexternalized.
candidates.assumptions: A user-specified set of interpretable nodes; the paper admits there is no precise definition of interpretable and suggests monitorability evaluations or training-incentive arguments.
candidates.relevance: Formalizes the 'CoT is necessary' premise of monitorability arguments. Its dependence on an undefined 'interpretable' node set shows where a formal legibility definition is missing.

candidates.title: Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography
candidates.authors: Sumeet Ramesh Motwani, Mikhail Baranchuk, Martin Strohmeier, Vijay Bolina, Philip H. S. Torr, Lewis Hammond, Christian Schroeder de Witt
candidates.formalism: security concepts (Cachin/Hopper-style steganography) in a multi-agent setting
candidates.formal_object: Formalizes secret collusion among generative agents using steganography, the incentives for it, and the capabilities it requires. The abstract describes a formalisation and an evaluation framework, not a new security definition.
candidates.assumptions: Communicating LLM agents; an overseer of a shared channel.
candidates.relevance: Imports classical steganographic security into LLM multi-agent settings. Useful framing; the precise definitions should be checked in the full text.

candidates.title: Preventing Language Models From Hiding Their Reasoning
candidates.authors: Fabien Roger, Ryan Greenblatt
candidates.formalism: information theory (channel capacity)
candidates.formal_object: Encoded reasoning is defined informally (intermediate steps encoded in a way not understandable to readers). Formal only as the capacity of the encoder-paraphraser-decoder channel, used to evaluate paraphrasing defenses.
candidates.assumptions: A known payload M and a decoder; a paraphraser defense.
candidates.relevance: Source of the encoded-reasoning concept. Its formal part measures hidden-message capacity, not whether hidden content is used as reasoning.

candidates.title: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Debate
candidates.authors: Jonah Brown-Cohen, Geoffrey Irving, Georgios Piliouras
candidates.formalism: complexity theory (doubly-efficient interactive proofs)
candidates.formal_object: Debate protocols in which the honest strategy needs only polynomially many simulation steps while verifying stochastic AI systems, even against a dishonest debater using exponentially many steps.
candidates.assumptions: Access to simulate the AI system; a polynomial-time judge.
candidates.relevance: Refines Irving et al. toward realistic computational costs. Superseded for obfuscation by prover-estimator debate.

gaps: Encoded reasoning as distinct from steganography: no definition requires the hidden content to be causally used by the model's computation. The steganographic gap and channel capacity measure usable or transmissible information, not reliance.

Obfuscation of CoT (suppressing or rewriting verbalized intent under monitor pressure): formal only by analogy, via DES opacity, planning goal obfuscation and debate's obfuscated arguments. No LLM-specific definition.

Legibility to humans as a concept: formal versions exist only relative to a verifier class (checkability) or an explicit observer model (goal inference). Opaque serial depth explicitly lacks a definition of an 'interpretable' node.

Causal monitorability: the information-theoretic definitions (Anwar, Baker, V-information) are observational and are satisfied by post-hoc CoTs. The only SCM-based quantity found is causal recall for binary interventions (Fu et al.).

Online or temporal monitorability for CoT (detection within bounded delay from a prefix): defined in runtime verification, DES diagnosability and Dragan's legibility, but not adapted to LLM reasoning.
